notes: Closing verse of chapter 2 (the segment has no colophon) and first use of 'brahmanirvāṇa' in the text (again at 5.24–26). antakāle 'pi, 'even at the time of death', links the state to the last moment (cf. 8.5); the commentators add: all the more if it is reached earlier in life.

paraphrase: Chapter 2 opens the teaching. 2.1–10 (frame): Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness and unmanliness (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma — he cannot fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, would rather live on alms, does not know which outcome is better — and asks Kṛṣṇa, as his disciple who has come for refuge, to tell him for certain what is better (śreyas) (2.4–8); he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, answers (2.9–10). 2.11–30: the teaching on the embodied self (dehin): the wise do not grieve; the self was never not and will never cease; it passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as through garments; what is not (asat) has no being and what is (sat) no non-being; the self neither slays nor is slain, is unborn, eternal, uncuttable, unmanifest and unthinkable; even on the contrary view birth and death are inevitable; therefore do not grieve. 2.31–38: the argument from one's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a dharmic battle is the kṣatriya's best good and a door to heaven, refusal brings sin and disgrace; fight treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. 2.39: transition — the understanding (buddhi) given 'in sāṃkhya' is now given 'in yoga'. 2.40–53: the yoga of understanding (buddhi-yoga): resolute understanding is one (2.41); the flowery speech of those who delight in Vedic statements and seek heaven and power keeps understanding from samādhi; the Vedas concern the three guṇas, be free of them (2.42–46); your right is to action, not its fruits; yoga is sameness and skill in actions; the wise, yoked with understanding, abandon the fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth (2.47–51); when understanding passes beyond delusion and stands steady in samādhi, you will attain yoga (2.52–53). 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: he gives up all desires and is content in the self, unshaken by sorrow and pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger, withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.55–61); the chain from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger, delusion and loss of memory to ruin (2.62–63), and its reverse through mastered senses to serenity and steady understanding (2.64–68); the sage is awake where beings sleep, is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved, and without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.69–71); this is the brahmic state, reaching which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to answer Arjuna's grief and his request for the good, first by knowledge of the self, then by the discipline of action done with steady understanding, culminating in the portrait of the one whose wisdom is steady.

paraphrase: Chapter 3 answers the question of understanding versus action. 3.1–2: Arjuna asks why, if understanding (buddhi) is held superior to action, Kṛṣṇa urges him to terrible action, and asks for one decisive teaching. 3.3–9: Kṛṣṇa says he declared of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā) — the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and the yoga of action for the yogins; actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is not reached by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can stay without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make everyone act; restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy, while karma-yoga with the senses controlled and without attachment excels; do your allotted action, for the world is bound by action except action for sacrifice. 3.10–16: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice, telling them to nourish the gods and be nourished; who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eating the remains of sacrifice frees from fault; the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman and the imperishable must be kept turning. 3.17–18: for one who delights and is content in the self there is nothing that must be done. 3.19–26: therefore act unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for the holding together of the world (loka-saṃgraha), since people follow the best; Kṛṣṇa himself, needing nothing, keeps acting lest the worlds perish; the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant. 3.27–29: actions are done by the guṇas, and only one deluded by the sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra) thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is not attached. 3.30–32: resign all actions to Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are released, those who cavil are lost. 3.33–35: all beings follow their nature; attraction and aversion lie in wait in the sense-objects; one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding; restrain the senses first, know what is beyond understanding, steady the self by the self and slay desire. The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to show why Arjuna must act — action being unavoidable, sacrificial, exemplary and non-binding when done without attachment — and to name desire as what must be overcome.
